prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I would have come. When you called. But. I had the most beautiful pale pink rose. Its healthy stem was clenched between my teeth. And. Its thorns bit sharply into my tender wet flesh. So. I couldn't answer you. Still. My lips moved at you silently. They offered words you never heard. They screamed inside my crazed brain. Only. It could do nothing for you. In time the petals wilted. They blew away. And. They became compost in someone else's garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to snap its grip on me. Then. My teeth fell out. Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks. They had implanted themselves permanently. They were suckling on my softest tissues. And. Not long after they sprouted tiny shoots. They coiled their way down. I still held the memory of your call. And. The long stemmed beauty lodged next to it. They cleaved unto the long roots curling down my neck. My body held tight and listened. Hard.

Keywords: When, But, Its

outputs.L1:
I would have come when you called. But I held the most beautiful pale pink rose, its healthy stem clenched between my teeth, its thorns biting sharply into my tender, wet flesh. So I could not answer you.

Still, my lips moved toward you in silence. They offered words you never heard, words screaming inside my crazed brain. Only, they could do nothing for you.

In time, the petals wilted. They blew away and became compost in someone else’s garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to break its hold on me. Then my teeth fell out.

Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks. They had implanted themselves permanently, suckling on my softest tissues. Not long after, they sprouted tiny shoots and coiled their way downward.

I still held the memory of your call, and the long-stemmed beauty lodged beside it. They cleaved unto the long roots curling down my neck.

My body held tight and listened—hard.
outputs.L2:
I would have gone to you when you called.

But I was holding the loveliest rose between my teeth, pale pink and perfect, its strong green stem locked in my mouth. Its thorns pressed cruelly into the soft, wet skin there, biting deep. Because of that, I could not answer.

Even so, my mouth shaped silent replies for you. My lips formed words you never received. Inside my frantic mind, they were shouting. But none of it could reach you. None of it could help.

After a while, the petals drooped, loosened, and drifted off. Somewhere else, they broke down into soil for another person’s garden. The stem, hard and stringy, dried out. I clamped my teeth down, trying to break its hold on me.

Then my teeth came loose and fell away.

The thorns had sunk into my cheeks. They had made a permanent home there, feeding on the most delicate parts of me. Before long, small shoots began to grow from them. They twisted downward, curling and winding inside me.

I kept the memory of your call. Beside it remained that long-stemmed beauty, still lodged within me. Together they fastened themselves to the long roots spiraling down my neck.

My body gripped them close and listened with all its strength.
outputs.L3:
The speaker longed to answer the call, to lift their voice and send a response outward, but they could not. A pale pink rose was clenched between their teeth, beautiful and delicate to the eye, yet held there with a force that made speech impossible. Its softness was deceptive. Though the petals brushed against their lips like something tender, the stem pressed cruelly into their mouth, and every attempt to speak only drove the thorns deeper.

The words the speaker wished to say remained silent, trapped behind the rose. They formed and dissolved without ever being heard. The thorns tore at the inside of their mouth, turning the act of response into pain. What might have been an answer became instead a wound. The call passed by unanswered, not because the speaker had nothing to say, but because beauty itself had become an obstruction, lodged where language should have been.

As time passed, the rose began to decay. Its pale pink petals withered, darkened, and fell away. The flower lost its softness, its color, and its fragrance, but its violence did not disappear with its beauty. The stem remained. The thorns remained. Long after the rose had ceased to resemble a rose, its sharpness stayed embedded in the speaker, a remnant of something once lovely that had become inseparable from pain.

Eventually, the thorns seemed to take root inside the speaker’s body. They were no longer merely caught in the mouth; they spread inward, invasive and alive, as though the rose had found a way to survive by becoming part of the speaker. What had begun as a moment of silence and injury became a permanent presence, growing deeper with time. The speaker carried it within them, unable to remove it without tearing themselves apart.

And so the memory endured: the unanswered call, the pale rose, the beauty that hurt, the words that never reached anyone. Even after the flower had rotted away, its meaning remained lodged in the speaker like a thorn beneath the skin. The call continued to echo in memory, bound forever to the painful beauty of the rose and to the silence it had forced upon them.
outputs.L4:
When you called, I could not answer.

Not because I did not hear you. Your voice arrived clearly, as if it had crossed no distance at all. It entered the room before the ringing stopped, before my hand even reached for the receiver. It knew my name. It knew the old path through me. It struck the walls of my chest and came back changed, softer, pleading, familiar enough to hurt.

But by then the rose was already in my mouth.

I do not know who placed it there. Perhaps I did. Perhaps it had been growing for years, quietly, from a seed lodged beneath the tongue. At first it was only a taste: green, bitter, almost sweet. Then a stem. Then thorns. Then the impossible bloom, opening against my teeth with a wet red patience.

I tried to speak around it. I tried to say your name. The petals filled my mouth like velvet soaked in blood. Every syllable caught on them, folded inward, became something wordless and warm. The thorns pressed into my gums. One pierced the soft place under my tongue. Another fastened itself behind my lower lip. I could feel the flower learning me, mapping the dark cavern of my mouth as if it had found a garden there.

You called again.

The sound moved through me, and my silence answered in my place.

I wanted to tell you that I was here. That I had always been here, even when I seemed far away. I wanted to tell you that I remembered everything: the street after rain, your hand hovering but not touching mine, the last sentence you did not finish, the way goodbye can disguise itself as an ordinary pause. I wanted to say wait. I wanted to say forgive me. I wanted to say anything.

But the rose had rooted.

Its stem slid down my throat, delicate and invasive. I felt it descend with a living certainty, passing the place where words are made, passing the place where breath gathers before becoming speech. It wound itself around my ribs. It found the heart and leaned there, not cruelly, not gently, but with the blind insistence of something that only knows how to grow.

The bloom remained in my mouth, beautiful and obscene.

I could not spit it out. I could not swallow it. It was too lovely to destroy and too painful to keep, which is how certain memories survive. They arrive as beauty and remain as occupation. They take nourishment from the body that cannot release them. They perfume the air while their roots tighten in secret.

After a while, the ringing stopped.

The silence that followed was not empty. It was dense with everything I had failed to say. It stood in the room like another person. I listened to it breathe. I listened to my own breath moving through the petals, ragged and floral, transformed into the scent of something dying beautifully.

Days passed, or years. It became difficult to tell. The rose did not wither. Instead, it adapted. Its thorns dulled where my mouth had learned them. Its petals darkened, deepened, took on the color of old wounds. Sometimes, when I looked in the mirror, I could see the red edge of it between my lips, as though I were forever on the verge of speaking some enormous truth.

People asked why I was quiet.

I smiled carefully.

They thought silence was absence. They did not understand that silence can be crowded, that it can have texture, roots, a pulse. They did not know that a single unanswered call can become a living thing, that a missed connection can lodge itself in the body and continue there, blooming in the dark.

Even now, if you were to call again, I do not know what would happen.

Perhaps the rose would loosen. Perhaps it would flower wider, filling me completely. Perhaps your voice would reach through the petals and find the small, trapped creature of my answer still waiting there, alive after all this time.

Or perhaps I would only bleed more quietly.

What I know is this: your call did not vanish. It entered me. It became stem, thorn, blossom. It became the red weight behind my lips. It became the beauty I cannot remove.

And in the place where my answer should have been, the rose continues to grow.
outputs.L5:
**When, But, Its**

When we face a challenge, we often look for the right moment to act. That moment may not always be perfect, but taking a small step forward can still make a big difference. Every situation has its own difficulties, its own lessons, and its own opportunities.

But fear and doubt can sometimes stop us from trying. We may think we are not ready, or that the path ahead is too uncertain. However, growth often begins when we decide to move despite our worries.

Its true value lies not only in success, but also in the experience we gain along the way. When we keep learning, but refuse to give up, life reveals its best possibilities.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about wanting to answer someone’s call but being unable to speak because a rose is held in your mouth, with the image becoming increasingly grotesque and emotional.
counterfactuals.output:
When you call, the room fills with birds that have forgotten how to be birds. They fall upward, beating their soft clocks against the ceiling. The telephone trembles on the table like a small black animal dreaming of thunder.

I want to answer.

I want to say your name, to let it leave me whole, warm, human.

But there is a rose in my mouth.

At first it is almost beautiful: a red bloom clenched between my teeth, a lover’s joke, a stage trick, a promise made in another country. Its petals brush my lips like velvet eyelids. Its stem lies cool against my tongue. I think, perhaps, I can speak around it. Perhaps I can make a sound thin enough to pass through thorns.

The phone rings again.

The rose roots deeper.

Its stem lengthens down my throat, green and slick, curling around the bell of my voice. Thorns open like little knives. They find the soft places. They learn me. Every word I try to form snags and tears, becoming red threads, becoming pulp, becoming the wet, untranslatable alphabet of pain.

I hear you breathing on the other end, or imagine I do. That is worse. Your silence has hands. It reaches through the wire and touches my face.

I try to hum. The rose drinks it.

I try to cry out. The rose blossoms wider, obscene with fragrance, filling my cheeks until my jaw aches, until petals spill between my lips in clots of crimson silk. They fall onto my chest like pieces of a heart too delicate to keep beating. The table grows damp. The floorboards soften. The whole house leans toward me, listening.

Please, I think. Please understand. I am not refusing you.

But the rose has become a garden. Its roots braid through my ribs, tightening around each lung. Its leaves unfurl behind my eyes, greening the dark. Bees crawl from my gums, drunk and golden, dragging bits of my unsaid devotion on their legs. The thorns pierce outward through my cheeks, small bright horns of grief. My mouth is no longer a mouth but a vase, no longer a vase but a wound arranged for ceremony.

Still the phone rings.

Still I love you with the terrible politeness of the mute.

I lift the receiver at last. My hand is shaking. From my lips comes only the thick perfume of ruined flowers, a warm rain of petals, the faint clicking of thorns against teeth.

On the line, your voice says, Are you there?

And inside me, beneath the roots, beneath the blood-bright bloom, beneath the bees and the swallowed scream, something kneels.

Yes, it says.

Yes.

Yes.

But nothing reaches you except the sound of roses opening in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short piece of dark, visceral literary fiction in first person. It should center on a pale pink rose, silence, missed communication, thorns, teeth, and bodily transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
The rose arrived without a note.

Pale pink, almost flesh-colored, its petals clenched around a wet yellow heart. It lay on my doorstep in the morning silence, stem long and green as a vein, thorns beaded with dew. I knew it was from you because no one else had ever learned my address and then forgotten how to speak.

I brought it inside.

All day my phone lay faceup on the table, black and mute. I watched it the way one watches a mouth before bad news. Once, the screen shivered with my own reflection: my lips parted, my teeth too visible, my tongue pressed behind them like something wanting out. I typed your name. I typed, *Why?* I typed, *Come back.* Each message remained unsent, blue-white and trembling under my thumb, until I deleted them one by one.

The rose opened in the heat of the room.

By evening its perfume had thickened, sweet and rotten, filling my throat. I lifted it to my face and felt a thorn enter my finger. Such a little pain. Such a precise red bead rising to answer it. I put my finger in my mouth and tasted iron, garden soil, the old argument we never finished.

That was when I heard it: not a sound, but the shape of one missing. The silence between us had grown teeth.

They came first behind my gums, crowding forward, sharp and eager. My jaw ached. My tongue found new points where none had been. In the mirror my mouth looked fuller, darker. I smiled and saw a small animal smiling back.

The rose shed a petal.

Then another.

Each one landed softly on the sink, pink scraps of skin. My hands had begun to harden, the veins under them darkening to green. When I tried to call you, my fingers would not bend properly; they curled around the phone like roots around a stone. I opened my mouth to speak your name, but only a wet rasp came out, a sound like stems being twisted apart.

The last petal fell at midnight.

By then the thorns had broken through me—along my wrists, my throat, the tender insides of my arms. They rose from my skin with terrible patience. I stood in the center of the room, blooming and bristling, unable to reach you, unable to stop becoming the message.

In the morning, perhaps, you will find me on your doorstep.

No note.

Only silence.

Only my pale pink mouth, full of teeth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an experimental breakup monologue where the speaker says “I would have come when you called,” but explains their absence through a symbolic flower lodged in their mouth?
counterfactuals.output:
I would have come when you called.

I want that entered into the record before the door closes, before your face becomes one of those houses I pass at night and do not look into. I would have come when you called, with my coat half-buttoned, with one shoe untied, with my whole ridiculous heart dragging behind me like a suitcase with a broken wheel.

But there was a flower in my mouth.

Not a metaphor, not at first.

A flower. Stem down my throat. Petals packed against my teeth. Something pale and ceremonial, something that had no business blooming where speech should have been. Every time I tried to answer you, it opened wider.

You said my name once.

The flower opened.

You said it again.

Pollen filled my lungs.

Do you understand what it is to be summoned and to be all garden? To have a tongue, but no language; a body, but no permission; love, but only in the shape of choking?

I stood there with the phone lit in my hand, your voice coming through like a match struck in another room, and I could not say yes. I could not say wait. I could not say I am coming, I am coming, I am already breaking the laws of distance.

The flower had roots by then.

It had found the soft places. It had made a trellis of my ribs. It had learned my silences and improved them. You always said I was beautiful when I was quiet. I should have known then that quiet was a country you wanted me exiled to.

Still, I would have come.

I need you to know that.

Not because it changes anything. Not because knowing turns the key backward. Not because the night reassembles itself and I arrive at your door before you stop needing me.

I say it because absence has been telling my story in my voice.

Absence has been wearing my coat.

Absence has been sleeping on my side of the bed, explaining me badly.

It says I did not care.

It says I chose the dark.

It says I heard you crying and became stone.

But I was not stone. I was orchard. I was overgrown. I was a mouth full of impossible spring.

And you—  
you kept asking for a sentence.

One sentence.

Come over.  
Say something.  
Tell me you love me.  
Tell me this is not the end.

I tried.

God, how I tried.

But the flower was enormous by then, a funeral arrangement, a wedding bouquet, every apology I had swallowed coming back dressed as bloom. Its petals were soft as your wrists. Its thorns were exact. Its scent was the room where we first forgave each other and should not have.

You think I abandoned you.

Maybe I did.

Maybe a flower is just a prettier word for fear.

Maybe I liked having something to blame that was not my own mouth.

Maybe I cultivated it. Watered it with every unsaid thing. Let it grow because it was easier to choke than confess: I was tired of being needed only at the hour of your collapse. I was tired of arriving like emergency weather. I was tired of my love being measured by how quickly I could disappear from myself.

There. See?

Even now, petals.

Even now, the red dust of truth on my hands.

I would have come when you called, but I had become the place where all our dead tenderness was planted. And when I opened my mouth, it was not my voice that came out.

It was the flower.

It said: stay.

It said: leave.

It said: this is love.

It said: this is what love becomes when no one prunes it.

So I did not come.

And you survived.

And I survived.

Though survival is a small, mean word for two people standing on opposite sides of a ruined garden, pretending not to recognize what they buried there.

I am saying goodbye now.

Carefully.

With shears.

With both hands.

If I bleed, do not come.  
If I bloom, do not come.  
If you hear your name in the leaves tonight, do not answer.

It will only be the flower practicing my voice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting surrealist paragraph with fragmented sentences, repetition of “And” and “So,” involving a rose stem clenched between teeth, petals wilting, thorns taking root, and the memory of someone’s call.
counterfactuals.output: And the rose stem clenched between teeth. Bitter green. Blood-dark. And the petals wilting one by one against the tongue, soft as old apologies. So the mouth became a vase, and the vase became a grave. And the thorns took root in the gums, in the jaw, in the small black soil beneath the skin. So every word bloomed crooked. And somewhere, somewhere behind the rain-streaked wall of the skull, the memory of their call kept ringing. Not a voice anymore. Not a name. And the petals fell. And the thorns held fast. So the silence answered.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic horror vignette about unspoken words becoming trapped in the body, using the metaphor of a beautiful long-stemmed rose that injures and grows inside the narrator.
counterfactuals.output:
I never said it.

That was the beginning of the garden.

The words rose in me, warm and red, pressing their soft mouths to the backs of my teeth. They wanted light. They wanted air. They wanted to become sound and be done with me. But I swallowed them instead, each one with its thorn still hidden, each one folded tight as a bud.

At first, it was almost beautiful.

A pressure beneath the ribs. A sweetness in the throat. I thought grief had a fragrance, and perhaps it does. In the mornings I woke with the taste of petals on my tongue, velvet and iron. When I breathed, something green stirred inside me. When I laughed, a stem dragged softly against my lungs.

Then the rose began to grow.

It sent a long stem down through the dark of me, elegant as a dancer’s spine, cruel as a needle. It rooted in the soft red earth below my heart. Its thorns learned my shape. They hooked into muscle, kissed bone, opened tiny mouths in places no one could see.

I became careful.

I moved slowly so the flower would not tear me.

I spoke gently so the bloom would not shake.

People told me I seemed composed. They admired the pale calm of my face, the way I pressed a hand to my chest as if touched by tenderness. No one knew I was holding myself shut. No one knew that beneath my blouse a rose had climbed the trellis of my ribs, blooming larger each night, drinking what I would not confess.

The unsaid thing fed it.

Every time I saw you, another petal unfurled.

Every time you asked, “Are you all right?” and I smiled, another thorn bent inward.

By winter, I could feel it in my throat: the blossom, full and fragrant, trying to escape. Its stem had grown impossibly long, winding through me in a green spiral, piercing liver, lung, memory. At night I dreamed of opening my mouth and letting the rose emerge whole—beautiful, terrible, shining with my blood.

But when I woke, I was silent.

And silence is rich soil.

Now I do not know where I end and the rose begins. My pulse trembles in its petals. My breath snags on its thorns. If you lean close, you may smell it: something sweet, something rotting, something desperate to be named.

Please do not ask me what I meant to say.

If I answer, the flower will bloom.

And if it blooms, it will split me open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
